info.title: Open Life Quoting API (AU)
info.summary: A vendor-neutral contract for pricing Australian life risk cover.
info.description:
A contract an insurer implements so that adviser software can obtain quotes directly, in one
shape, without a per-insurer integration.

## What this is

Four operations. An insurer prices a set of covers for one insured (`POST /quotes`), describes
what it supports (`GET /capabilities`), and helps resolve an occupation to its own rating
manual (`GET /occupations`, `POST /occupations:match`).

The request is modelled on the questions an adviser actually answers, in the order they answer
them: who is being insured, the answers that apply to the whole policy, then one section per
benefit. It is deliberately not modelled on any existing engine's wire format.

## The rules that matter most

These guard against failures that are **silent** — they produce a plausible number rather than
an error, so nobody notices until a client complains.

1. **All six payment frequencies on every priced line.** Sub-annual premiums carry a frequency
   loading, so the monthly premium is not the annual over twelve. A consumer that divides will
   understate the cost and nothing will look wrong.
2. **Never price what you could not assemble.** If some requested covers cannot be written,
   return the line with `all_needs_met: false`, populated `errors` and no premium. A partial
   policy priced as though complete reads as the best offer on the table.
3. **Report every option you did not apply.** An option the product cannot honour appears in
   `resolved_options` as `unsupported_ignored`. Otherwise a quote that quietly dropped a
   benefit is indistinguishable from one that included it, and the adviser recommends the
   wrong product.
4. **Echo what you rated.** `resolved_occupation` and `rate_table_version` are what make a
   quote reproducible months later, which is what an adviser needs to justify a
   recommendation.

## Money

Amounts are decimal strings with an explicit currency, never JSON numbers. Premiums are summed
and compared to the cent, and JSON numbers are IEEE-754 doubles in JavaScript and in most
generated clients.

## Privacy

The request carries no name, no address, no contact details and no health data, and
`Insured` is a closed schema so there is nowhere to put them. Age is sent as age next birthday
rather than a date of birth wherever the insurer permits. This is a design constraint, not a
recommendation: a consumer sends the same client to several insurers, so every field
multiplies into several separate collections by several separate entities.

## Conformance

An implementation need not offer every cover or every option value. Declare what you offer in
`GET /capabilities` and the conformance suite tests you against that declaration. What is not
optional is the four rules above.

tags.name: Occupations
tags.description: Resolving an occupation to the insurer's own rating manual.

post.description:
Price the requested covers for one insured and return every line the insurer can offer, plus the lines it had to decline.
### What a response means
One request yields MANY lines. An insurer with two brands and a campaign on one of them may answer a single life-cover request with three lines. Consumers must treat the response as a set of comparable offers, never as "the price".
### Three things a consumer must not do
- **Do not derive a frequency.** Every line carries all six. `annual / 12` is not the monthly
  premium, because sub-annual premiums carry a frequency loading.
- **Do not price a failed line.** A line with `all_needs_met: false` carries no `premiums` and
  is not an offer. It exists so the adviser can see that this insurer was asked and could not
  write the combination.
- **Do not assume an option was applied.** Check `resolved_options`. An option the product
  cannot honour appears there as `unsupported_ignored`, and the premium does not include it.

### Caching
Quote responses carry personal information about the insured and MUST NOT be cached by intermediaries. Servers MUST send `Cache-Control: no-store`.

200.description: The quote was produced. Note that a 200 does not mean every requested cover was priced — inspect `all_needs_met` and `resolved_options` per line.

get.description:
Describe the covers, option values, brands, campaigns and optional features this implementation offers.
A consumer calls this once and caches it. It drives which controls an adviser is offered, so an unsupported combination can be prevented rather than rejected after the fact.
This is the mechanism that makes a partial implementation conformant: an insurer that writes four covers and three waiting periods declares exactly that, and the conformance suite tests it against what it declared rather than against the whole standard.
Consumers MUST NOT treat this document as authoritative. Hand-maintained capability documents drift from the pricing engine, so the runtime paths — 422 `unsupported-value` and `resolved_options` — stay mandatory regardless of what is declared here.

ETag.description: Entity tag for the document. Servers SHOULD supply it and honour `If-None-Match`, so consumers can revalidate cheaply instead of re-fetching.

Cache-Control.description: Servers SHOULD permit caching for at least one hour — this document changes when a product range changes, not per request.

304.description: Not modified — the consumer's cached copy is current.

get.summary: Search this insurer's own occupation list
get.description:
Return the occupations this insurer rates, in its own wording, each with its rating matrix.
This exists so an adviser can correct one insurer's occupation by hand. The usual flow resolves an occupation once via `POST /occupations:match`, but where the match is imperfect — or where the adviser knows this insurer's product better — they need to search the insurer's own list and choose. That choice is then sent as `occupation.insurer_occupation_id` on the next quote, and the insurer rates on it without re-matching.
Returning the rating matrix inline is deliberate: it lets a consumer show the consequence of a change before spending a pricing call on it.
An empty `q` returns the whole list, paged, so a consumer can pre-load it.

200.description: Matching occupations. An empty array is a valid answer and means this insurer rates nothing matching the query — not that the query was malformed.

Cache-Control.description: Occupation lists change rarely; servers SHOULD permit caching for at least an hour. The response carries no personal information, so it is safe to cache.

post.summary: Resolve a baseline occupation to this insurer's own
post.description:
Given an ABS OSCA code and the qualifiers that sit beneath it, return the insurer's own occupations that correspond, most confident first.
### Why this endpoint exists
An adviser picks an occupation once, from one picker, and expects to compare every insurer on the panel. Each insurer rates its own list, so something has to bridge the two. Putting the bridge here — inside the insurer, which is the only party that knows its own manual — avoids making anyone else the custodian of a mapping they cannot maintain.
### An empty result is a real answer
`candidates: []` means this insurer has no occupation corresponding to the reference. The consumer MUST show the insurer as unquotable for this client and MUST NOT substitute a nearby occupation of its own choosing. A silently wrong occupation produces a wrong premium that looks entirely normal, and an adviser has no way to detect it.
### Confidence
Where the insurer maintains a one-to-one correspondence to the baseline it returns `exact`. A match derived from qualifiers alone will usually be `moderate` or below, and a consumer SHOULD ask the adviser to confirm anything below `exact` rather than pricing straight through.
Results depend only on the occupation reference, never on the insured, so they are safely cacheable by the consumer per insurer.

oauth2.description:
OAuth 2.0 client credentials (RFC 6749, section 4.4). Machine-to-machine only.

The consumer is a system, not a person, so there is no interactive flow: an authorisation
code flow would oblige insurers to provision and maintain an account per adviser, and to
answer "is this adviser appointed with us?" on every token request.

Insurers who need adviser or licensee attribution — for distribution reporting or campaign
entitlement — should take it from the token's own claims or from the client registration,
not by pushing identity into the quote request.

Servers SHOULD publish an RFC 8414 metadata document so consumers can discover the token
endpoint rather than having it configured by hand. mTLS MAY additionally be required.

IdempotencyKey.name: Idempotency-Key
IdempotencyKey.description:
A consumer-generated UUID identifying this logical request. Replaying the same key with an identical body MUST return the stored response rather than re-pricing; replaying it with a different body MUST fail with 409 `idempotency-conflict`. Servers SHOULD retain keys for at least 24 hours.
Pricing is computationally idempotent but commercially metered — many insurers count quotes, and some bill on them. This header is what stops a network timeout and retry from being counted twice, which protects both sides.

RequestId.name: X-Request-Id
RequestId.description: Consumer-supplied correlation identifier. Echoed on the response; the server generates one if absent.

OccupationQuery.name: q
OccupationQuery.description:
Free-text search over the insurer's own occupation descriptions. Matching is implementation-defined; servers SHOULD match on substrings of any word rather than a prefix of the whole string, since advisers search on the distinguishing word ("painter") rather than the leading one.
An absent or empty `q` returns the full list, paged. That is deliberate — consumers pre-load the whole list to build a picker.

Cursor.name: cursor
Cursor.description: Continuation token from the previous page's `page.next_cursor`.

Limit.name: limit
Limit.description: Maximum items per page. A server MAY return fewer for its own reasons, so completion is signalled only by the absence of `page.next_cursor`.

ClientReference.title: ClientReference
ClientReference.description:
The consumer's own reference for the person being quoted, echoed back on the response so a quote can be reconciled against the requesting system.
This MUST be a pseudonymous token, not a name, email, customer number or anything else that identifies the person outside the requesting system — the recommended construction is an HMAC of the internal record id under a per-insurer salt. Deriving it per insurer means two insurers cannot correlate their request streams to reconstruct a consumer's client base, and it keeps the request within data-minimisation obligations.

Gender.title: Gender
Gender.description: The gender used for rating. Life insurance rate tables in this market are published for two values, so this enum carries only those two; it describes a pricing input, not the insured's identity, and it is deliberately separate from any demographic field a CRM might hold.

AustralianState.title: AustralianState
AustralianState.description: State or territory of residence. Required because stamp duty on life insurance is levied per jurisdiction, so the same cover carries a different total depending on this value.

EmploymentStatus.title: EmploymentStatus
EmploymentStatus.description: The insured's working status. This is a rating input in its own right, not a duplicate of the occupation: disability covers (`income_protection`, `business_expenses`, `tpd`) generally require a working status, and a working occupation paired with a non-working status is a contradiction that many insurers answer with a nil premium rather than an error. Consumers SHOULD reconcile the two before quoting. The `working` set is `employee` and the three `self_employed_*` values; the remainder are non-working.

Decimal.title: Decimal
Decimal.description: A fixed-point decimal amount serialised as a string, with at most two fractional digits. Scientific notation, thousands separators, currency symbols and leading `+` are not permitted. Implementations MUST NOT normalise `"0.00"` to `"0"` or vice versa when echoing a value back — but consumers MUST treat the two as numerically equal.

Money.title: Money
Money.description: An amount of money. Currency is carried explicitly even though this standard is Australia-only, so a future market does not become a breaking change.

currency.title: CurrencyCode
currency.description: ISO 4217 alphabetic code. Only AUD is defined by this version of the standard.

NonNegativeMoney.title: NonNegativeMoney
NonNegativeMoney.description: Money that cannot be negative — sums insured, premiums, stamp duty, policy fees. A negative value here is always a defect, so it is rejected at the schema boundary rather than surfacing as a nonsensical premium.

OccupationQualifiers.title: OccupationQualifiers
OccupationQualifiers.description: The risk discriminators that sit beneath an occupation code. Every field is optional, and an absent field means "not stated" rather than "no" — an insurer SHOULD rate an unstated qualifier at its own default and MUST NOT infer a favourable answer from silence.

trade_qualified.description: Whether the insured holds a recognised trade or professional qualification for the occupation. Frequently the difference of one or more rating classes in the trades.

working_height_m.description: The greatest height above ground at which the insured routinely works, in metres. `0` means they do not work at height. Insurers commonly band this (for example at 10m).

works_offshore.description: Routinely works offshore or on vessels, including oil and gas platforms.

manual_duties_percent.description: Proportion of working time spent on manual duties, 0-100. The usual axis distinguishing a white-collar rating from a light- or heavy-manual one within the same occupation.

hours_per_week.description: Ordinary hours worked per week. Most income-protection products require a minimum (commonly 20-25 hours) before they will offer the full benefit basis.

licensed_to_carry_firearm.description: Carries a firearm as a requirement of the occupation.

OccupationRef.title: OccupationRef
OccupationRef.description:
How a consumer names an occupation. At least one of `osca`, `anzsco` or `insurer_occupation_id` MUST be present.
`insurer_occupation_id` is the authoritative form: it names a row in the insurer's own list and removes all matching ambiguity, so it is what a consumer SHOULD send once the adviser has confirmed a per-insurer occupation. The others ask the insurer to match, and the insurer MUST report what it matched to.
THE BASELINE FORMS ARE ASPIRATIONAL, AND CONSUMERS MUST NOT ASSUME THEM. `osca` and `anzsco` describe where this standard wants the market to get to: a taxonomy owned by the ABS rather than by any party in the value chain, so one occupation picker serves every insurer. That is the right destination and it is not where the market is. No rating engine we have examined speaks OSCA — engines carry their own occupation lists and match against them internally — so an implementation supporting `insurer_occupation_id` alone is fully conformant and is expected to be the common case for some time.
The practical consequence for a consumer: read `occupation_resolution` in the capability document before sending a baseline code, and be prepared to resolve via `GET /occupations` or `POST /occupations:match` first. Sending `osca` to an insurer that does not accept it is a 422, not a quote.
What would change this is insurers publishing `osca` on the rows of their own occupation lists — see `InsurerOccupation.osca`, which exists precisely so the correspondence can be built up from the insurer side rather than imposed on it.

osca.title: OscaCode
osca.description: ABS Occupation Standard Classification for Australia code. Six digits, optionally hyphenated at the four-digit unit-group boundary for readability.

anzsco.title: AnzscoCode
anzsco.description: Legacy ANZSCO code, accepted as an alias for consumers and manuals still using it. Ignored when `osca` is present.

insurer_occupation_id.description: An identifier from this insurer's own occupation list, as returned by `GET /occupations`. Opaque; scoped to the insurer. When present, the insurer MUST rate on exactly this occupation and MUST NOT re-match.

employment_basis.description:
For an insured who is NOT in paid work. Send this INSTEAD of an occupation code.
OSCA classifies occupations, so it has no code for a retired or home-duties client — yet these are real, quotable lives: home-duties TPD is a standard product, and a non-working spouse is a routine case. Before this existed the schema required an occupation code that does not exist, and an implementer facing a closed schema would send the nearest working code — producing the silently-wrong-occupation failure this contract warns about everywhere else.
An insurer MUST rate on this rather than attempting to match it to an occupation, and MUST echo it in `ResolvedOccupation.employment_basis`.

description.description: The adviser-facing description shown on screen, for display and diagnostics only. NON-NORMATIVE: an insurer MUST NOT rate on this string.

Insured.title: Insured
Insured.description: The person whose risk is being priced. Exactly one of `age_next_birthday` or `date_of_birth` MUST be present; `age_next_birthday` SHOULD be preferred.

age_next_birthday.description: The insured's age at their next birthday, which is the basis life rate tables are indexed on in this market. Bounds are the widest any product issues at; individual products declare their own limits in the capability document.

date_of_birth.description: Full date of birth, RFC 3339 full-date. Send only where the insurer has declared it necessary — see the privacy note at the head of this file.

smoker.description: Whether the insured meets the insurer's definition of a smoker. Definitions differ between insurers (typically on the lookback period and on whether occasional or non-tobacco nicotine use counts), so this is the consumer's answer to the insurer's own question rather than an objective fact. Insurers SHOULD publish their definition in their documentation.

annual_income.description: Gross annual income before tax. Required to price income protection and business expenses, which are capped as a proportion of it, and used by some insurers to band occupation ratings for white-collar roles. Omit where no income-based cover is requested.

Structure.title: Structure
Structure.description:
How the premium behaves over the life of the policy.
  - `stepped`   re-rated each year as the insured ages
  - `level_65`  held level (bar indexation and rate changes) to age 65, then stepped
  - `level_70`  as above, to age 70
  - `blended`   a stepped/level mix, where the insurer blends the two rate bases
`blended` is incompatible with indexation on some products; where an insurer cannot honour it, that is reported as `unsupported_ignored` rather than silently substituted.

Ownership.title: Ownership
Ownership.description:
Who owns the cover, which determines the tax treatment, whether the premium can be paid from superannuation, and which side of the super/non-super premium split each amount falls on.
  - `super`           held inside a retail superannuation fund
  - `ordinary`        held personally, outside super
  - `smsf`            held inside a self-managed superannuation fund
  - `superlink`       split structure: one benefit part-owned inside super, part outside,
                      linked so the parts cannot be claimed twice
  - `smsf_superlink`  the same split structure where the super side is an SMSF

PremiumWaiver.title: PremiumWaiver
PremiumWaiver.description: Whether to include the waiver-of-premium option, which suspends premiums while the insured is disabled. `prefer` is a DEFERRED CHOICE — the adviser is asking the insurer to include it where the product allows and to price without it where not, and the insurer MUST report which it did in `resolved_options`.

Percentage.title: Percentage
Percentage.description:
A percentage serialised as a decimal string (not a 0-1 ratio): `'25'` means 25%. At most three fractional digits, and at most 1000.
A string for the same reason as `Decimal` and `RatePerThousand`. This was a JSON number until 0.2.0, justified on the grounds that percentages are inputs to arithmetic rather than amounts stored to the cent, and that three decimal places are exactly representable. The second half of that is not true: `0.001` has no exact IEEE-754 representation, so a loading of `25.001` arrives as `25.000999...` in every generated client. More to the point, the reasoning proved too clever — a loading percentage IS an input to pricing, and it was the one remaining path by which a contract value reached a rating engine through a double while every amount beside it travelled as a string. The inconsistency was visible in this very file: `RatePerThousand` is the OTHER axis of the same loadings map and was always a string.
`'0'` is a MEANINGFUL value — see the loadings schema, where an explicit zero cancels an inherited loading and is not the same as omitting the field. Implementations MUST NOT normalise `'0'` to `'0.000'` or vice versa when echoing a value back, and consumers MUST treat the two as numerically equal.

RatePerThousand.title: RatePerThousand
RatePerThousand.description: A dollar rate applied per $1,000 of sum insured, the second axis on which underwriting loadings are expressed. Serialised as a decimal string for the same reason as `Decimal`.

Loadings.title: Loadings
Loadings.description:
Underwriting loadings the adviser expects the insurer to apply, expressed per benefit on two independent axes. Both axes may apply to the same benefit, in which case the insurer applies both.
SPARSE-MAP SEMANTICS, NORMATIVE. These maps are sparse and every present key is meaningful:

  - a benefit ABSENT from a map carries no loading on that axis;
  - a benefit present with a value of `'0'` carries an EXPLICIT nil loading.

The two are NOT interchangeable. An implementation MUST NOT normalise a `'0'` into an omission or an omission into a `'0'`, and MUST NOT reject `'0'` as pointless — a consumer sends it to state positively that this benefit is not loaded, which is a different instruction from declining to say. JSON Schema cannot express this constraint, which is precisely why it is stated here and tested by the conformance suite.
Keys are `CoverType` values, restricted to the five benefits a loading can attach to. Needle stick and child trauma have no loading axis and MUST be rejected as keys.
A key names a cover TYPE, so it applies to EVERY cover of that type in the request. Where a request holds two covers of one type and they need different loadings, set `loadings` on the individual covers instead — a cover-level entry replaces the policy-level one for that cover.
A key naming a cover type not present in `covers` MUST be rejected with 422 `invalid-combination` rather than silently ignored: it is far more likely to be a mistake than an intention.

percentage.description: A percentage uplift on the risk premium for that benefit. `'25'` means the premium is loaded by 25%.

rate_per_thousand.description: A flat dollar amount per $1,000 of sum insured, added to the risk premium for that benefit. Not applicable to the monthly-benefit covers on every product; insurers report an inapplicable axis via `resolved_options`.

PolicyDefaults.title: PolicyDefaults
PolicyDefaults.description:
The answers that apply to the policy as a whole. Every field is optional and every field has a defined default, so a minimal request is valid; a cover may override any of them for itself.
On a quote screen these controls are usually drawn inside the first benefit's panel, because that is where an adviser looks for them. They are hoisted here deliberately: an insurer should not have to know that the policy-wide premium structure is to be read off the life cover.

structure.description: Default premium structure for every cover. Defaults to `stepped`.

ownership.description: Default ownership for every cover. Defaults to `ordinary`.

premium_waiver.description: Default waiver-of-premium answer for every cover. Defaults to `exclude`.

CoverId.title: CoverId
CoverId.description: CLIENT-assigned identifier for one requested cover, unique within the request. It does two jobs: a rider names its parent with it (`linked_to`), and every priced line echoes it so the consumer knows which requested cover produced which priced cover without inferring from cover type and amount.

CoverType.title: CoverType
CoverType.description: The benefits an adviser can ask to be priced, in the order they are presented on a quote screen. A cover may be requested standalone or, for some combinations, as a rider linked to a parent cover — see `link_type` on the cover schemas.

Preference.title: Preference
Preference.description: The general three-state answer to an optional benefit: leave it out, put it in, or let the insurer decide (`prefer`). Every `prefer` in a request MUST come back as an entry in `resolved_options` saying what was actually applied.

CoverLoadings.title: CoverLoadings
CoverLoadings.description: Loadings for a single cover, on the same two independent axes as the policy-level map. Both may apply at once.

percentage.description: A percentage uplift on this cover's risk premium.

rate_per_thousand.description: A flat dollar amount per $1,000 of sum insured, added to this cover's risk premium.

LinkType.title: LinkType
LinkType.description: How a cover relates to the cover named in `linked_to`. `extension` means the cover is held as a rider on the parent and its benefit reduces the parent's when paid, which is what makes it cheaper than the same cover held standalone.

CoverBase.title: CoverBase
CoverBase.description: Fields common to every cover. `ownership`, `structure` and `premium_waiver` are OPTIONAL here: omitted, they inherit the request's policy-level answer, which is how the quote screen behaves. Supplying one overrides it for this cover only.

pay_by_rollover.description: Whether the premium may be funded by a rollover from another superannuation fund. Only meaningful where `ownership` resolves to a superannuation type; insurers MUST report it as `unsupported_ignored` rather than silently dropping it otherwise.

loadings.description:
Underwriting loadings for THIS cover, overriding the policy-level map.
Needed because the policy-level map is keyed by cover TYPE, and two covers of the same type in one request are routine — a standalone TPD alongside a linked TPD extension, or life inside super alongside life outside it. A single `{tpd: 50}` was then ambiguous: apply it to both, to the first, or to the standalone only? Three conformant implementations, three different premiums, and nothing in `resolved_options` obliged to disclose which reading was used, because from the insurer's point of view the loading WAS applied as asked.
Where present this replaces the policy-level entry for this cover entirely — it does not merge.

linked_to.description: The `cover_id` of the parent cover, when this cover is held as an extension of it. MUST reference a cover present in the same request, MUST NOT be self-referential, and the graph of links MUST be acyclic. Absent means the cover is standalone.

LifeCover.title: LifeCover
LifeCover.description: A death benefit paid as a lump sum. May be the parent of TPD and trauma extensions.

TpdDefinition.title: TpdDefinition
TpdDefinition.description:
Which test of total and permanent disability applies, in descending order of how favourable it is to the insured.
  - `own_occupation`  unable to work in their own occupation
  - `any_occupation`  unable to work in any occupation they are suited to
  - `home_duties`     the domestic-duties test, for a non-working insured
  - `adl`             the activities-of-daily-living test
  - `prefer`          let the insurer apply the best definition the occupation allows
Availability is occupation-dependent: an insurer that cannot offer the requested definition for the rated occupation reports it via `resolved_options`.

PreferenceQuad.title: PreferenceQuad
PreferenceQuad.description: A four-state answer to an optional benefit, for the cases where an adviser wants to express a leaning rather than a decision. `prefer_exclude` and `prefer_include` are DEFERRED: the insurer settles them and MUST report what it applied in `resolved_options`.

TpdCover.title: TpdCover
TpdCover.description: Total and permanent disability, as a lump sum. Held standalone, or as an extension of a life or trauma cover via `linked_to`. `life_buyback` and `double_benefit` are only meaningful on an extension, since both describe what happens to the parent cover when this benefit is paid.

life_buyback.description: Reinstatement of the parent cover after this benefit is paid. Extensions only. A subset of `LifeBuyback` — `after_3_years` is not offered on a TPD extension.

double_benefit.description: Whether this benefit is paid IN ADDITION to the parent cover rather than reducing it. Extensions only; materially increases the premium.

BenefitQuality.title: BenefitQuality
BenefitQuality.description: Which end of a product range to select from where an insurer offers several tiers of the same benefit. This is a preference over the insurer's OWN range, not a cross-insurer ranking, and it is resolved by the insurer.

TraumaCover.title: TraumaCover
TraumaCover.description: Critical illness cover, as a lump sum. Held standalone or as an extension of a life cover.

life_buyback.description: Reinstatement of the parent cover after this benefit is paid. Extensions only. A subset of `LifeBuyback` — `immediate` is not offered on a trauma extension.

double_benefit.description: Paid in addition to the parent cover rather than reducing it. Extensions only.

reinstatement.description: Whether the trauma benefit itself can be reinstated after a claim, allowing a later unrelated condition to be claimed again.

child_care_benefit.description: An additional benefit payable on complications of pregnancy or childbirth, or on a child's serious illness, depending on the product. Only offered where the insured's gender makes the pregnancy component applicable, so insurers commonly report this as `unsupported_ignored` otherwise.

benefit_quality.description: Which tier of the insurer's trauma range to select from.

WaitingPeriod.title: WaitingPeriod
WaitingPeriod.description: How long the insured must be disabled before a monthly benefit starts to accrue. Shorter periods cost materially more. Not every product offers every value; an insurer declares the values it supports in its capability document and rejects the rest with 422 `unsupported-value`.

BenefitPeriod.title: BenefitPeriod
BenefitPeriod.description: How long a monthly benefit continues to be paid once a claim is admitted. The `age_*` values pay to that age, which for a younger insured is far longer — and dearer — than any of the fixed terms.

ReplacementRatio.title: ReplacementRatio
ReplacementRatio.description: The proportion of pre-disability income the monthly benefit is intended to replace, used to select between product variants that differ on this basis. `any` lets the insurer offer whatever its product supports.

IncomeProtectionCover.title: IncomeProtectionCover
IncomeProtectionCover.description: A monthly benefit while the insured is disabled and unable to earn. The benefit is capped as a proportion of `annual_income`, so that field is required on the insured whenever this cover is requested.

monthly_benefit.description: The monthly amount sought, before any cap the insurer applies.

indexed_claim_benefit.description: Whether a benefit in payment is indexed against inflation.

accident_benefit.description: Whether the benefit starts from the date of an accident rather than after the full waiting period.

superannuation_contribution.description: An additional monthly amount to cover superannuation contributions while on claim. Absent means none.

BusinessExpensesCover.title: BusinessExpensesCover
BusinessExpensesCover.description: Reimbursement of fixed business overheads while the insured is disabled. Benefit periods are short by nature — this covers the cost of keeping a practice open, not the loss of income.

waiting_period.description: A subset of `WaitingPeriod` — the long deferral periods are not offered on this benefit.

benefit_period.description: A subset of `BenefitPeriod` — cover for business overheads is short by nature.

NeedleStickCover.title: NeedleStickCover
NeedleStickCover.description: A lump sum on occupationally acquired blood-borne infection. Offered to healthcare occupations only, so an insurer will commonly answer this with an unavailable line for anyone else.

InsuredChild.title: InsuredChild
InsuredChild.description: A child named on a child trauma cover. Deliberately narrower than `Insured`: children are rated on age and gender alone, so nothing else is collected.

child_id.description: Consumer-assigned identifier, unique within the cover, so per-child results and per-child validation errors can be attributed without relying on array position.

ChildTraumaCover.title: ChildTraumaCover
ChildTraumaCover.description: Critical illness cover on named children. The amount is per child, so this cover carries no cover-level sum insured — each child names their own.

CoverRequest.title: CoverRequest
CoverRequest.description: One cover to be priced. Which fields are permitted is determined entirely by `cover_type`; each variant is closed, so an option that belongs to another cover is a validation failure rather than something an implementer has to remember to ignore.

RequiredFeatures.title: RequiredFeatures
RequiredFeatures.description:
Product features the insured requires, as a filter on which products may be used. A product that does not offer every feature named for a benefit MUST NOT be used to write that benefit.
THIS IS A FILTER, NOT AN OPTION. The difference matters: an option asks the insurer to add something and is answered in `resolved_options`; a filter narrows the product set BEFORE pricing, so the honest answer to "no product has this" is a line with `all_needs_met: false` and a populated `errors`, not a cheaper line quietly written without the feature. An insurer MUST NOT satisfy a required feature by ignoring it.
Keys are `CoverType` values, and the codes under each are the insurer's own, discoverable from `features` on that cover in the capability document. A code that is unknown to the insurer, or that is not scoped to the benefit it appears under, MUST be rejected with 422 `unsupported-value` rather than ignored — an adviser filtering on "must include terminal illness" and silently getting products without it is the failure this exists to prevent.
Absent or empty means no filter, which is the overwhelmingly common case.

ProjectionIndexation.title: ProjectionIndexation
ProjectionIndexation.description:
How sums insured grow across a projection. A single rate applies to every cover that can be indexed.
Not every benefit can be. Where a product does not index a cover the insurer MUST say so in `excluded_covers` on the projection it returns, rather than silently projecting a flat sum insured inside an indexed projection — the totals would otherwise be unattributable.

rate.description: Annual indexation rate as a percentage. `'5'` grows each indexed sum insured by 5% a year, compounding.

ProjectionRequest.title: ProjectionRequest
ProjectionRequest.description:
Ask for the cost of each line projected forward, as well as its price today.
Needed because a stepped premium rises every year, so the first-year price is a poor basis for a recommendation and a level premium that looks dear today is often cheaper over the term an adviser is actually advising on. Comparing two structures on their first-year premiums alone is the mis-comparison this exists to remove.
Optional to implement. An insurer that cannot project declares `projections: false` in its capability document; if it is asked anyway it MUST price the quote normally, omit `projection` from every line, and report it once in `resolved_options` with `option: projection` and `unsupported_ignored`, rather than failing the quote.

years.description: Project this many years forward, inclusive of the current year.

to_age.description: Project to the insured's stated age. Where this is at or below the insured's current age the request is a 422 `invalid-combination` — an empty projection is not a useful answer.

indexation.description:
Whether to grow each cover's sum insured over the projection, and by how much.
Absent means no indexation: the projection prices today's sums insured at each future age, which is what "what will this policy cost me at 55" asks. Present, it prices a policy whose cover keeps pace, which is a different and equally legitimate question — but the two are not comparable, so an insurer MUST report which it applied.

QuoteRequest.title: QuoteRequest
QuoteRequest.description: A request to price one or more covers for one insured. A response to this is a set of priced lines, not a single price: an insurer may return several lines for one request where it has more than one brand, product combination or campaign variant that satisfies the covers asked for.

covers.description:
The covers to price. Only covers the adviser has switched on appear here — an absent cover type is not requested, and there is no "included: false" form.
`cover_id` MUST be unique across the array. Where a cover names a parent with `linked_to`, the parent MUST also be present; order within the array is NOT significant and a server MUST NOT require parents to appear first.

campaign_codes.description:
Campaign or discount variants to price in ADDITION to the insurer's standard rates. Each requested campaign the insured qualifies for yields its own line, so the adviser can compare the standard offer against the discounted one rather than being silently given whichever is cheaper. An empty array or an absent field means standard rates only.
Codes are the insurer's own, discoverable from its capability document. An unknown code is a 422 rather than being ignored, so a mistyped campaign cannot look like an ineligible one.

QuoteId.title: QuoteId
QuoteId.description: Opaque, server-assigned identifier for a whole quote response. Required so a quote can be retrieved, audited and reproduced later — an adviser must be able to justify a recommendation years after making it.

LineId.title: LineId
LineId.description: Opaque, server-assigned identifier for one priced line within one quote. Unique within its `QuoteId`. Consumers MUST treat it as opaque and MUST NOT parse it. It is the key for per-line follow-up calls such as the unmet-needs diagnostic.

InsurerId.title: InsurerId
InsurerId.description: Stable identifier for the issuing insurer, assigned by this standard's registry so it is the same value at every implementer. Lowercase, hyphenated.

BrandId.title: BrandId
BrandId.description: Stable identifier for the brand a line is sold under. Equal to the `InsurerId` where the insurer sells under a single brand. REQUIRED on every priced line even from a single-insurer endpoint, because one insurer commonly issues several brands and a consumer must not have to infer the brand from a product name.

ProductName.title: ProductName
ProductName.description: The insurer's own marketing name for a product, verbatim, for display only.

RateTableVersion.title: RateTableVersion
RateTableVersion.description: The insurer's identifier for the pricing basis used for this line — a rate table version, effective date, or equivalent. REQUIRED for reproducibility: without it, "why is this premium different from the one we quoted last month" is unanswerable, which is the single most common audit question and the field insurers least often expose.

PremiumBreakdown.title: PremiumBreakdown
PremiumBreakdown.description:
One frequency's premium, split by whether it is funded inside or outside superannuation and with stamp duty shown separately on each side.
ARITHMETIC INVARIANT, NORMATIVE AND TESTED:

  total == premium_super + stamp_duty_super + premium_non_super + stamp_duty_non_super

exactly, to the cent, with no tolerance. `policy_fee` is INCLUDED within `total` and within whichever premium component bears it — it is not a further addition. Keeping the fee outside the total is a recurring source of comparison tables that understate the real cost.
The super/non-super split is a genuine split, not a bucketing: one cover can carry both sides at once where it is written under a linked ownership structure.

total.description: The all-in amount payable at this frequency.

premium_super.description: Premium funded from superannuation, excluding stamp duty.

premium_non_super.description: Premium funded outside superannuation, excluding stamp duty.

stamp_duty_super.description: Stamp duty attributable to the superannuation-funded premium.

stamp_duty_non_super.description: Stamp duty attributable to the non-superannuation premium.

policy_fee.description:
The policy or administration fee at this frequency, GROSS of stamp duty — that is, the fee plus the duty levied on it, so it is the amount by which `total` exceeds the sum of the cover lines.
Gross is stated explicitly because the two conventions differ by the duty rate and are indistinguishable in the payload. One insurer reporting the fee net and another gross makes a "premium excluding fees" figure, or any fee-to-fee comparison, silently wrong — and the difference is small enough to look like a product variation rather than a units error.
Where the split matters, `policy_fee_premium` and `policy_fee_stamp_duty` give it exactly.
Reported separately from the cover lines because the fee is not attributable to any one cover, so it cannot be recovered by summing them.

policy_fee_premium.description: The fee itself, excluding duty. Optional; where present, plus `policy_fee_stamp_duty` it MUST equal `policy_fee`.

policy_fee_stamp_duty.description: Stamp duty levied on the policy fee.

PremiumSet.title: PremiumSet
PremiumSet.description:
The same line priced at all six payment frequencies. ALL SIX ARE REQUIRED.
An insurer must not return only the frequency it was asked for, because there is no way to derive the others: sub-annual premiums carry a frequency loading, so `weekly x 52 >= fortnightly x 26 >= monthly x 12 >= quarterly x 4 >= half_yearly x 2 >= annual`. Returning all six also means a consumer can let an adviser switch frequency without re-pricing, which removes a whole class of billable round-trips.
ROUNDING. The ordering holds on the UNROUNDED amounts. Once each frequency is rounded to the cent the products can cross by up to one cent per period — a $1,000 annual premium at zero loading gives monthly 83.33 (annualising to 999.96) and quarterly 250.00 (1,000.00), so monthly annualises BELOW quarterly. A consumer checking the ordering MUST therefore allow a tolerance of `periods x $0.01`; a conformance test without it fails every honest zero-loading insurer.
An insurer that levies no frequency loading returns six sets whose annualised totals are equal within that tolerance; that is valid.

CoverTypeResponse.title: CoverTypeResponse
CoverTypeResponse.description:
RESPONSE-facing CoverType. Same meaning as `CoverType`, but extensible: a consumer MUST pass an unrecognised value through for display rather than failing, so that adding to the benefits is a minor release rather than a major one.
Known values: [life, tpd, trauma, income_protection, business_expenses, needle_stick, child_trauma]. Validate against `CoverType` when SENDING; tolerate anything when RECEIVING.

OwnershipResponse.title: OwnershipResponse
OwnershipResponse.description:
RESPONSE-facing Ownership. Same meaning as `Ownership`, but extensible: a consumer MUST pass an unrecognised value through for display rather than failing, so that adding to the ownership forms is a minor release rather than a major one.
Known values: [super, ordinary, smsf, superlink, smsf_superlink]. Validate against `Ownership` when SENDING; tolerate anything when RECEIVING.

StructureResponse.title: StructureResponse
StructureResponse.description:
RESPONSE-facing Structure. Same meaning as `Structure`, but extensible: a consumer MUST pass an unrecognised value through for display rather than failing, so that adding to the premium structures is a minor release rather than a major one.
Known values: [stepped, level_65, level_70, blended]. Validate against `Structure` when SENDING; tolerate anything when RECEIVING.

CoverLine.title: CoverLine
CoverLine.description:
One priced cover within a line. `cover_id` is echoed from the request so a consumer can match a priced cover to the one it asked for without guessing from type and amount.
THE AMOUNT FIELD DEPENDS ON THE COVER. Income protection and business expenses are written as a MONTHLY BENEFIT and carry `monthly_benefit`; every other cover carries `sum_insured`. Before this distinction existed, `sum_insured` was the only option and an insurer had to choose how to report a $6,500-a-month benefit — as `6500.00` or annualised to `78000.00`, both conformant. A consumer comparing benefits across a panel was comparing incompatible units with nothing to disambiguate them, and a 12x discrepancy reads as a product difference rather than an error.

cover_id.description: Echoed from the request. Absent only where the insurer added this cover of its own accord because the product requires it.

cover_type.description: Extensible on the response side — see `CoverTypeResponse`. Pass an unrecognised value through rather than failing.

description.description: The insurer's own name for this cover as written.

sum_insured.description: The lump sum actually written, which may differ from the amount requested where the insurer applied a cap or a product minimum. Any such difference MUST also appear in `resolved_options` as `substituted`. Present on every cover EXCEPT income protection and business expenses.

monthly_benefit.description: The MONTHLY benefit actually written — not annualised. Present on income protection and business expenses, and on nothing else. Where the insurer capped it below the amount requested, that MUST also appear in `resolved_options` as `substituted`.

waiting_period.description: The waiting period as WRITTEN, for the monthly-benefit covers. Reported here as well as in `inclusions` because the as-written terms are what a consumer compares, and `inclusions` is optional, free-text-keyed, and therefore not something to depend on.

benefit_period.description: The benefit period as written, for the monthly-benefit covers.

tpd_definition.description: The TPD test as written. An own-occupation and an any-occupation TPD at the same sum insured are materially different cover, so a consumer comparing two lines needs this structurally rather than having to parse it out of display text.

linked_to.description: Echoed from the request where this cover was written as an extension.

premiums.description: This cover's contribution to the line's premium, at all six frequencies. The same arithmetic invariant applies per cover. Summing `cover_lines[].premiums[f].total` will NOT reach the line total wherever a policy fee applies — read the line total, do not derive it.

CoverRating.title: CoverRating
CoverRating.description: One cell of an insurer's occupation rating matrix: the class it would rate this occupation at for one benefit, and whether that benefit is available to the occupation at all.

supported.description: Whether this benefit can be offered to this occupation. `false` means the occupation is uninsurable for this benefit — distinct from a poor rating class.

rating_class.description: The insurer's own class code. INSURER-SCOPED: class "1" at one insurer has no defined relationship to class "1" at another, and consumers MUST NOT compare, sort or average this value across insurers. Absent when `supported` is `false`.

rating_class_label.description: A human-readable rendering of the class, for display where the code is cryptic.

OccupationRatings.title: OccupationRatings
OccupationRatings.description: An insurer's rating of one occupation across every benefit it offers. Keys are `CoverType` values, except that TPD is split by definition because a single occupation is routinely ratable under one TPD test and uninsurable under another.

tpd_home_duties.description: The domestic-duties TPD test. Present because it is the only TPD basis available to a non-working insured, so omitting it left exactly the clients `employment_basis` exists for with no way to learn whether they are insurable.

needle_stick.description: Availability here is purely occupation-driven — the benefit is offered to healthcare occupations and nobody else — which makes it precisely the case this matrix exists to pre-answer. Without the key an insurer had nowhere to say `supported: false`, and a consumer had to spend a pricing call to find out.

ResolvedOccupation.title: ResolvedOccupation
ResolvedOccupation.description: What the insurer actually rated on. REQUIRED on every priced line, because a quote whose occupation cannot be reproduced cannot be audited, and because a wrong occupation produces a wrong premium that looks entirely normal.

insurer_occupation_id.description: The row rated. Absent only where `employment_basis` was used, since a non-working basis is not a row in the insurer's occupation list.

employment_basis.description: Echoed when the insured was rated on a non-working basis rather than an occupation. Exactly one of this or `insurer_occupation_id` is present.

description.description: The insurer's own wording for what it rated.

match_confidence.description: How confident the insurer is in the match, when it matched from a baseline code rather than being given `insurer_occupation_id`. `exact` means a maintained one-to-one mapping. Consumers SHOULD surface anything below `exact` to the adviser for confirmation rather than pricing silently.

ResolvedOption.title: ResolvedOption
ResolvedOption.description:
What became of one requested option. An entry is REQUIRED for every option the insurer did not apply exactly as asked, and for every deferred choice (`prefer`, `prefer_include`, `prefer_exclude`, `any`) whether or not the outcome matched the leaning.
NORMATIVE: any option present in the request but NOT reflected in this array with an `applied` value equal to the requested value MUST be reported here — and an option the product cannot honour at all MUST be reported as `unsupported_ignored`. An insurer that silently ignores an option produces a line that looks like it included a benefit it did not, which is the most consequential defect this standard exists to prevent.

cover_id.description: The cover the option was given on, echoed from the request. Use the literal `policy` for an option given at policy level.

option.description: The field name of the option, as it appears in the request schema.

requested.description: The value the consumer asked for. Absent where the consumer did not supply one.

applied.description: The value the insurer actually priced. Absent where the option was ignored entirely.

detail.description: Why, in adviser-facing terms. RECOMMENDED whenever the resolution is `unsupported_ignored`, and for `substituted` it is what lets an adviser judge whether the substitution is acceptable.

InclusionGroup.title: InclusionGroup
InclusionGroup.description: One grouping of as-priced settings — typically one per cover written.

field.description: The name of the setting, as a standard field path where one applies (for example `waiting_period`), so a consumer can label it in its own vocabulary.

value.description: The as-priced value. A standard enum value where one applies.

display_label.description: The insurer's own wording, where it wants a specific rendering.

ProjectionBasis.title: ProjectionBasis
ProjectionBasis.description: What the insurer actually projected, which is not always what was asked. An insurer that applied a different indexation rate, or could not index some covers, says so here rather than in `resolved_options`, because the answer is only interpretable alongside the numbers.

years.description: How many years the projection covers, matching the length of `years`.

indexed.description: Whether sums insured were grown across the projection.

indexation_rate.description: The annual rate actually applied. REQUIRED when `indexed` is `true` — including where the insurer applied its own default because the request named no rate, which is the case a consumer most needs told.

excluded_covers.description:
`cover_id`s that were NOT indexed because the product does not index them, while the rest of the projection was. Empty or absent means every cover was treated alike.
Real products do this — a child trauma benefit is commonly flat inside an otherwise indexed policy — and without this field those covers' premiums are simply lower than a consumer's own recalculation would predict, with nothing to attribute the difference to.

year.description: Offset from the current year. `0` is the year being quoted.

age_next_birthday.description: The insured's age next birthday in that year, so a consumer can label the series by age rather than by offset. Omitted where the request carried no age the insurer can advance.

annual_total.description: The all-in cost for that year — premium plus stamp duty plus policy fee, on the same basis as `PremiumBreakdown.total` at annual frequency.

cumulative_total.description: The running total up to and including this year. Stated rather than left to the consumer because rounding each year and summing gives a different answer from summing and rounding once, and two consumers doing it differently is a comparison table that disagrees with itself.

sum_insured_indexed.description: Whether this year's figure reflects an indexed sum insured. Distinguishes the first year of an indexed projection, which is normally unindexed, from the rest.

Projection.title: Projection
Projection.description:
One line's cost projected forward, year by year, with the running total.
The year-by-year series is returned rather than a single headline number because a consumer presents this several ways — average annual cost, cumulative cost, first year, final year — and every one of those is derivable from the series. Returning only a total would force a re-quote per presentation, which is what advisers do today.
THE BASIS MUST BE ECHOED. A projection with indexation applied and one without are different questions with different answers, and a consumer comparing an indexed projection from one insurer against a flat one from another gets a difference that has nothing to do with price.

total.description: The cumulative cost over the whole horizon — the final year's `cumulative_total`, repeated here so a consumer showing only the headline need not walk the series.

years.description: One entry per projected year, ordered from `year: 0` (the current year, whose `annual_total` MUST equal the annual figure in `premiums`) and contiguous thereafter.

Score.title: Score
Score.description: A research score from 0 to 100 inclusive, as a decimal string with at most two places.

ResearchScores.title: ResearchScores
ResearchScores.description:
Third-party research ratings for a line, as published by a research house.
NOT THE INSURER'S OWN OPINION, and the standard is deliberate about that. An insurer that scored its own products here would be marking its own homework, so `provider` is REQUIRED and a consumer that cannot attribute a score should not display it. Scores are only comparable between lines rated by the same provider on the same dataset.
Optional throughout. Most insurers will not carry these at all; an aggregator or a research licensee may.

provider.description: The research house whose ratings these are.

dataset_version.description: The provider's identifier for the dataset the scores came from. Scores move when a provider republishes, so without this a stored score cannot be reproduced or defended — the same reasoning as `rate_table_version`.

feature_score.description: The product's feature rating, 0 to 100, where higher is more comprehensive. A measure of what the product covers, independent of price.

combined_score.description: The provider's blended rating of features against price, 0 to 100. Deliberately separate from `feature_score`: they answer different questions and a consumer sorting on the wrong one recommends the wrong product.

LineDocument.title: LineDocument
LineDocument.description:
A document or link relating to one quote line.
Modelled as a typed list rather than as named fields so a new document type is a new enum value rather than a schema change, and so an insurer offering none simply returns an empty array.
URLS MAY BE SHORT-LIVED AND MAY CARRY AUTHORITY. A `continue_application` link in particular can resume a quote inside the insurer's own system, so it MUST be treated as a credential: consumers MUST NOT log it, embed it in a shared document, or hand it to anyone who is not the adviser who requested the quote. An insurer SHOULD set `expires_at` on any link that grants access rather than issuing one that lives forever.

media_type.description: The document's media type, e.g. `application/pdf`. Omit for a link to a web page, where the answer is `text/html` and saying so adds nothing.

title.description: The insurer's own name for the document, for display.

expires_at.description: When the URL stops working. RFC 3339 with an explicit offset. Absent means the insurer makes no commitment either way, which a consumer should read as "do not store this".

QuoteLine.title: QuoteLine
QuoteLine.description: One row of a comparison table: one product or product combination, from one brand, at one campaign variant.

component_products.description: The insurer's own names for each product this line was assembled from, where a line combines more than one. Display only.

all_needs_met.description:
Whether the insurer assembled EVERY cover requested. `false` means it could not, and `errors` MUST then be non-empty and `premiums` MUST be absent.
This is not an error response. The insurer was able to answer; the answer is that this combination cannot be written. Consumers MUST NOT present such a line as a price, MUST NOT include it in a cheapest-first sort, and MUST NOT allow it to be selected.

errors.description: Why the requested covers could not be assembled, in terms an adviser can act on ("the linked TPD amount cannot exceed the life cover"). Non-empty exactly when `all_needs_met` is `false`.

premiums.description: The price of this line at every payment frequency. REQUIRED on a line where `all_needs_met` is `true`; MUST be absent otherwise.

cover_lines.description: The priced covers making up this line, one per cover the insurer wrote. Includes covers the insurer added of its own accord where a product requires them.

resolved_options.description: What the insurer did with every option that it decided rather than simply obeyed. See `ResolvedOption` — this array is how a consumer learns that an option was dropped.

campaign.description: The campaign variant this line was priced under. Absent on a standard-rates line.

name.description: The insurer's own wording for the campaign, for display.

medical_requirements.description:
Mandatory medical underwriting this insurer requires before it will issue THIS line, in the insurer's own wording. Requirements scale with the sum insured, so two lines from the same insurer can legitimately differ.
An EMPTY array means "none required" and is a positive statement. It is distinct from `underwriting_reported: false`, which means the insurer has not told us either way — a consumer MUST NOT render the latter as "no medicals required".

underwriting_reported.description: Whether `medical_requirements` is a complete answer for this line.

inclusions.description: The line's as-priced configuration, as structured values rather than rendered text, so a consumer can display it in its own words. Read from what the insurer actually wrote, which differs from the request wherever a deferred choice was settled.

projection.description: This line's cost projected forward. Present only where the request asked for a projection and the insurer can produce one; a line where `all_needs_met` is `false` MUST NOT carry one, since there is no premium to project.

research_scores.description: Third-party research ratings for this line, where the insurer publishes them.

documents.description: Documents and links relating to THIS line — the product disclosure statement, a branded quote report, a deep link into the insurer's own system to continue the application.

QuoteResponse.title: QuoteResponse
QuoteResponse.description: The result of a pricing request: every line the insurer can offer for the covers requested, plus the lines it had to decline. Lines are a FLAT array, never a map keyed by brand or product — one brand routinely produces several lines once campaigns are in play.

quoted_at.description: When the quote was priced. RFC 3339 with an explicit offset.

valid_until.description: When these premiums cease to be reliable. Advisory but strongly RECOMMENDED: without it a consumer cannot tell a stale saved quote from a current one.

client_reference.description: Echoed verbatim from the request, so the response can be reconciled.

lines.description: Every line the insurer produced, priced and unpriced alike. MAY be empty, which means the insurer offers nothing at all for this insured — a legitimate answer, not an error.

warnings.description: Adviser-facing notes that apply to the whole quote rather than one line. For information only: a warning MUST NOT be the sole indication that something was not priced as asked — that belongs in `resolved_options` or `errors` on the affected line.

type.description: A URI identifying the problem kind. Use a registered value from `ProblemType` where one applies. Consumers branch on this field; `title` and `detail` are for humans.

title.description: A short, human-readable summary of the problem kind. Stable per `type`.

status.description: The HTTP status code, repeated here so a logged problem is self-contained.

detail.description: A human-readable explanation specific to this occurrence. MUST NOT contain personal information about the insured — problem documents are logged widely on both sides.

instance.description: A URI reference identifying this specific occurrence.

request_id.description: The value of the `X-Request-Id` header for the failed request, echoed so a consumer can quote one token when asking the insurer to investigate.

errors.description: Field-level detail, present on validation failures. Each entry MUST carry a JSON Pointer to the offending member of the request body, so a consumer can highlight the exact control that was wrong rather than showing a whole-form error.

pointer.description: RFC 6901 JSON Pointer into the request body.

value_supplied.description: The rejected value, echoed for diagnosis. Omit where it is sensitive.

values_supported.description: The values that would have been accepted. Populating this turns a failed integration attempt into a self-service fix.

examples.title: Unsupported value
examples.detail: This product does not offer a 730 day waiting period.

CoverCapability.title: CoverCapability
CoverCapability.description: What one cover type supports. `supported_options` carries VALUE SETS rather than a list of field names, so an insurer can narrow an enum — three waiting periods out of seven — without the standard needing a new version.

can_extend.description: The cover types this cover may be written as an extension of, named with `linked_to`. An empty array means it is only available standalone.

supported_options.description: Permitted values per option field, keyed by the field name as it appears in the cover schema. An option field ABSENT from this map is not supported at all for this cover and MUST be reported as `unsupported_ignored` if sent.

features.description:
Named product features that may be required for this cover via `required_features`.
DISTINCT FROM `supported_options`, and the distinction is the whole point. An option is something the consumer asks the insurer to APPLY, and the insurer answers it in `resolved_options`. A feature is something the consumer FILTERS on, and the insurer answers it by using only products that have it — or by declining the benefit. So the same underlying product capability may legitimately appear in both, and they are not interchangeable.
Codes are the insurer's own and scoped to this cover: the same code under a different cover is a different feature, and a code used under the wrong cover MUST be rejected.

name.description: The insurer's own wording, for display in a feature picker.

Frequency.title: Frequency
Frequency.description: How often the premium is paid. A premium at a sub-annual frequency is NOT the annual premium divided by the number of periods: insurers apply a frequency loading, so `monthly x 12 >= annual`. Every priced product therefore carries all six frequencies — see `PremiumSet` — and consumers MUST read the frequency they need rather than deriving it.

Capabilities.title: Capabilities
Capabilities.description: What this implementation supports. Cacheable — servers SHOULD send an `ETag` and a `Cache-Control` max-age of at least an hour, and consumers SHOULD revalidate rather than fetching on every quote.

spec_version.description: The version of this standard the implementation is built against, as a semver string. A consumer compares this against its own to decide which optional features to use.

brands.description: The brands this endpoint can price. More than one is normal and is why `brand_id` is required on every line even from a single-insurer endpoint.

covers.description: One entry per cover type offered. A cover type absent from this array is not offered at all, and a request for it MUST be answered with 422 `unsupported-cover`.

frequencies.description: Which payment frequencies the insurer's own billing supports. Note this does NOT narrow the response: `PremiumSet` requires all six regardless, because a consumer compares and annualises across insurers. This field says which ones a policy can actually be BILLED at.

split_frequency_supported.description: Whether the superannuation and non-superannuation portions of one policy can be billed at different frequencies.

occupation_resolution.description: Which forms of `OccupationRef` this implementation accepts. `insurer_occupation_id` MUST always be supported; the others are optional, and an implementation that supports none of the baseline forms requires consumers to resolve an occupation via `/occupations` first.

occupation_qualifiers_used.description: Which `OccupationQualifiers` fields actually affect this insurer's rating. Lets a consumer avoid collecting facts that will not change the answer.

features.description: Optional parts of the standard this implementation provides.

line_diagnostics.description: Whether the per-line unmet-needs diagnostic endpoint is implemented.

projections.description: Whether `projection` on the request is honoured. An implementation declaring `false` that is asked anyway MUST still price the quote — see `ProjectionRequest`.

projection_indexation.description: Whether a projection can grow sums insured. Separate from `projections` because projecting today's cover forward is materially easier than indexing it, and an insurer that can do the first is not thereby claiming the second.

required_features.description: Whether `required_features` is honoured. An implementation declaring `false` MUST reject a request carrying one with 422 rather than pricing it unfiltered — a filter silently not applied returns products the adviser expressly excluded.

research_scores.description: Whether lines carry third-party research ratings.

documents.description: Whether lines carry documents or application links.

campaigns.description: Campaign variants that can be named in `campaign_codes`.

requires_authorisation.description: Whether this campaign is only available to consumers specifically authorised for it. An unauthorised request for it is a 403, not a silently standard-rated line.

target_p95_latency_ms.description: The latency the insurer expects to meet at `max_concurrent_requests`. Consumers of several insurers at once fan out in parallel and are bounded by the slowest, so this figure determines whether a consumer must apply a shorter timeout than its own overall budget.

Cursor.title: Cursor
Cursor.description: Opaque continuation token. Consumers MUST treat it as opaque, MUST NOT construct one, and MUST NOT assume it remains valid indefinitely — a server MAY expire cursors and answer an expired one with 400 `invalid-request`.

InsurerOccupation.title: InsurerOccupation
InsurerOccupation.description: One row of the insurer's occupation list, carrying the rating matrix so a consumer can show what a change of occupation would do before re-pricing.

description.description: The insurer's own wording, shown to the adviser verbatim.

osca.description: The baseline code this row corresponds to, where the insurer maintains the correspondence. Publishing it is what allows a consumer to pre-resolve occupations in bulk rather than calling `:match` per quote.

requires_employment_status.description: An employment status this occupation implies, where one is mandatory. A non-working occupation paired with a working status is the commonest cause of a nil premium, so an insurer that constrains this SHOULD say so here.

effective_to.description: Absent while the row is current. A past date means the row is closed to new business.

PageInfo.title: PageInfo
PageInfo.description: Continuation state for a paged collection. Absence of `next_cursor` is the ONLY reliable signal that a walk is complete — consumers MUST NOT infer completion from a short page, because a server may return fewer items than requested for its own reasons.

OccupationMatchRequest.title: OccupationMatchRequest
OccupationMatchRequest.description: Ask the insurer which of its own occupations corresponds to a baseline reference.

OccupationCandidate.title: OccupationCandidate
OccupationCandidate.description:
One candidate match — an insurer occupation plus how confident the insurer is that it corresponds to the reference it was given.
Declared standalone rather than as `allOf: [InsurerOccupation, {match_confidence}]`, which is what it was in 0.1.0 and which was UNSATISFIABLE: `InsurerOccupation` closes itself with `additionalProperties: false`, and that keyword only sees its own `properties` — so it forbade the very fields the second branch required. No object could satisfy both, and the only conformant response was an empty `candidates` array, which this contract defines as "no matching occupation, treat the insurer as unquotable". The endpoint that bridges the shared baseline to each insurer's manual was therefore impossible to implement, and `redocly lint` reported the document valid.
The lesson generalises: `additionalProperties: false` composed under `allOf` is nearly always a bug. Where composition is genuinely wanted, use `unevaluatedProperties: false` on the composed schema — as `covers.yaml` does correctly.

description.description: The insurer's own wording, shown to the adviser verbatim.

osca.description: The baseline code this row corresponds to, where the insurer maintains it.

match_confidence.description: How confident the insurer is. `exact` means a maintained one-to-one correspondence to the baseline. A consumer SHOULD ask the adviser to confirm anything below `exact` rather than pricing straight through.

match_detail.description: Why this candidate was proposed, and which qualifiers drove it. Worth populating: it is what lets an adviser choose between two plausible rows.

OccupationMatchResponse.title: OccupationMatchResponse
OccupationMatchResponse.description:
Candidate matches, most confident first.
An EMPTY `candidates` array is a valid and important answer: it means the insurer has no occupation corresponding to the reference given. A consumer MUST treat that as unquotable for this insurer and MUST NOT fall back to a nearby occupation of its own choosing — a wrong occupation produces a wrong premium that looks entirely normal, which is worse than a visible gap.

XRequestId.description:
Correlation identifier, echoed from the request or generated by the server when the request did not carry one. REQUIRED on every response, including errors.
This is not ceremony. A consumer of several insurers investigating "the premium was wrong last Tuesday" has to be able to hand one token to one insurer's support desk; without it, the only shared identifier is a timestamp.

SpecVersion.description: The version of this standard the response was produced against. Lets a consumer detect an implementation that has moved without announcement.

BadRequest.description: The request could not be parsed, or a value was structurally invalid. Problem type `invalid-request`.

Unauthorized.description: No access token was presented, or it was malformed or expired. Problem type `unauthenticated`.

Forbidden.description: The token is valid but lacks the scope required for this operation, or names a campaign the consumer is not authorised for. Problem type `forbidden`.

Conflict.description: An `Idempotency-Key` was reused with a different request body. Problem type `idempotency-conflict`.

UnprocessableEntity.description:
The request was well formed but cannot be priced as asked — an unsupported cover, an unsupported option value, or a combination the product does not permit. Problem types `unsupported-cover`, `unsupported-value`, `invalid-combination`, `incomplete-request`.
NOTE the boundary: this status is for a request the insurer will not accept. An insurer that accepts the request but cannot assemble the covers returns 200 with the line flagged `all_needs_met: false`.

TooManyRequests.description: Rate limit exceeded. Problem type `rate-limited`. `Retry-After` is REQUIRED — without it a consumer fanning out across several insurers has no basis for a backoff and will retry into the limit.

ServiceUnavailable.description: A dependency of the pricing engine is unavailable. Problem type `upstream-unavailable`. Distinguished from `internal-error` so a consumer can retry this and not that.
